newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Arab "holy warriors" in Afghan refugee camp siege.
newsitem.headline: Arab "holy warriors" in Afghan refugee camp siege.

text.p: Three well-armed self-styled Arab holy warriors are holding out in a an Afghan refugee camp near the northwestern Pakistani town of Peshawar after killing two people, camp officials said on Monday.
They said two Egyptians and an Algerian had used machineguns and hand-grenades for two days to keep away camp guards seeking to arrest them for the killings.
"These people are totally mad," the camp's Afghan commander Haji Dost Mohammad said. "We are trying to arrest them alive but we will have to kill them if there is no other way out."

The three are veterans of the Afghan guerrilla war against Soviet occupation in the 1980s and belong to a shadowy Tafkiri group that regards Moslems going under U.S. influence as infidels and liable to be put to death, Pakistani security officials said.

The radical group had fled to Afghanistan after Pakistani authorities launched a hunt for them in a border tribal region in April 1993 but returned after the Taleban Islamic militia took control of eastern Afghan provinces bordering Pakistan.

The present standoff at the large Jalozai camp, housing some 200,000 refugees, began when the group killed an Algerian fellow member, Mustapha Algazairee, after he refused to join their "jihad" (holy war) and decided to surrender to authorities, withness said. An Afghan was also killed by a stray bullet.
Three other Egyptians also fell out from the group and surrendered, camp sources said.
The incident coincided with a one-day Islamic summit conference in the Pakistan capital Islamabad, which was also attended by leaders from pro-Western Arab countries.
Dost Mohammad said he had asked Pakistani police for help but they had refused to join the operation.

"The group has hoisted black flags on their houses and are refusing to surrender," a Pakistani official said. "They believe in martyrdom and will continue to fight until they die or run out of ammunition."
The Jalozai camp is controlled by Ittehad-i-Islami group of Afghan leader Abdurrab Rasul Sayyaf, who is regarded as close to Saudi Arabia.
